title: Detection Strategy for Email Bombing
summary: This strategy detects email bombing, the delivery of a large volume of messages to one mailbox in a short time so that the real message is buried. It maps to T1667 Email Bombing. The technique is interesting because the flood is rarely the goal: it hides a password reset, a new payee confirmation or a purchase receipt from the person reading the inbox. Detection relies on mail gateway and mailbox telemetry that reports per-recipient message rates, sender diversity and subscription confirmations, joined to identity and finance audit events in the same window. The main failure mode is that the flood is delivered by legitimate bulk senders, so a volume rule alone pages the service desk about marketing mail while the actual fraudulent account change passes unnoticed.

beginner.definition: This detection finds a mailbox that suddenly receives a very large number of messages. The sender is often a normal mailing list or newsletter signup page. The goal of the attacker is to bury one important message under hundreds of useless ones.
beginner.whyItMatters: People notice a password reset message. They do not notice it when three hundred newsletters arrive in the same hour. While the mailbox fills up, the intruder can approve a payment change or reset an account. The victim may also lose real mail that is pushed out of the inbox.
howItWorks: The mail gateway records every accepted message, including the recipient address and the sender domain.
A rule counts messages per recipient over a short window, such as ten minutes.
It also counts how many different sender domains wrote to that recipient in the same window.
If both counts cross a threshold, the mailbox is flagged as flooded.
The rule then looks for account or payment changes for the same user and raises the alert with both facts joined.
beginner.example: Imagine a shop till receipt that is stamped three hundred times in one hour for tiny amounts. The one real purchase is hidden in the middle of the roll. The cashier has to search through the whole roll to find it.
takeaways: Email bombing is usually cover for another action, not the action itself.
Volume alone is normal; volume plus a change to the account or a payment is the real signal.
Ask the user what they were doing when the flood started, because the useful detail is often only in their memory.

objectives: Define email bombing and explain why the message flood is a distraction technique
Identify per-recipient volume and sender-diversity metrics available from a mail gateway
Correlate a mailbox flood with password reset, mailbox rule and payment change events for the same user
Distinguish bulk marketing mail from an abusive signup flood using sender reputation and domain age
Choose thresholds that fit the size and normal volume of each mailbox group
dataSources: Mail gateway message tracking logs with recipient address, sender domain and delivery timestamp
Mailbox audit events for inbox rule creation and mailbox forwarding configuration changes
Identity provider audit events for password reset, multi-factor factor change and new device enrolment
Helpdesk or service desk ticket records tagged as mailbox volume complaints
Subscription confirmation email logs from bulk senders identified by their sending reputation records
logic: The detection measures message count per recipient and the number of distinct sender domains per recipient inside a short window, then joins that spike to identity or financial change events for the same account in a wider window. A normal heavy mail day comes from a small number of known bulk senders and is not followed by account changes. An abusive flood comes from many newly seen or unrelated domains, often generated by automated signup forms, and frequently precedes or accompanies a password reset or a bank detail change. The correlation is what separates the two, because neither the volume nor the account change is unusual on its own.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Mailbox flood followed by identity or payment change
# logsource:
#   product: email
#   service: gateway
# detection:
#   selection_flood:
#     action: accepted
#     timeframe: 10m
#     groupby: recipient
#     threshold: count(messages) by recipient > 200 and count(unique sender_domain) > 50
#   selection_change:
#     event_type:
#       - password_reset
#       - mfa_factor_change
#       - payee_added
#   condition: selection_flood and selection_change
# level: high
falsePositives: Marketing campaigns sent to a distribution list that shares one mailbox address
A user who subscribes to many status pages and alerting services during an incident
Mail loops between two automated systems that generate bounces and delivery reports
A mailbox that receives an approved bulk import of historical messages during a migration
tuningNotes: Set thresholds per mailbox group rather than globally, because a shared support mailbox legitimately receives far more mail than an executive mailbox. Maintain an allow list of known bulk sender domains with good reputation and exclude them from the distinct sender count, which removes most marketing noise. Alert at a lower volume when the flood is followed by a mailbox rule creation or a payment change, since that combination is rare. Accept that a determined attacker can stay just under the threshold; complement the rule with a daily report of the top twenty recipients by sender diversity so slow floods still surface.
